Where is 'A Letter to God' set, and how does the setting matter to the plot?
questions.answer: The story is set on a small isolated farm on the crest of a low hill in Mexico — the only farmhouse for miles. The setting matters in three ways: (i) the FARM is dependent on a single CROP — a single hailstorm can destroy a whole year's livelihood. (ii) The ISOLATION (one house for miles) means Lencho has no neighbours to turn to — he must turn to GOD. (iii) The SMALL POST OFFICE in the valley is the only link between Lencho and the world — making it the crucial place where the story's twist plays out.

questions.question: Describe how the rain turned into a hailstorm and what damage it caused.
questions.answer: The rain that the family had been waiting for began as a heavy downpour — welcomed by the family as a sign of a good harvest. Without warning the rain turned into a HAILSTORM, with hailstones the size of ACORNS. The storm continued for an HOUR, leaving the field WHITE — as if covered with salt. Not a leaf remained on the trees and the corn was TOTALLY DESTROYED. The single hour of hail wiped out a year's livelihood for Lencho's family.

questions.question: Why does Lencho write a letter to God, and what does this show about him?
questions.answer: After the hailstorm has destroyed his crop, Lencho's family is devastated. But Lencho has ONE HOPE that does not depend on weather or neighbours: he believes GOD WILL HELP. So he sits down that night and writes a letter to God asking for ONE HUNDRED PESOS to plant his fields again and live till the next harvest. He addresses the envelope simply 'To God' and posts it. This shows: (i) his UNSHAKEABLE FAITH — he doesn't pray quietly, he writes a direct letter; (ii) his PRACTICAL nature — he names a specific amount with a specific purpose; (iii) his SIMPLE conviction — he doesn't need a long address.

questions.question: How does the postmaster respond to Lencho's letter, and what does his response show?
questions.answer: The postmaster first LAUGHS when he sees the letter — addressed simply 'To God'. But his expression soon changes. He decides he does not want to SHAKE Lencho's faith in God, so he treats the letter SERIOUSLY. He asks his employees to contribute money for Lencho and adds part of his OWN SALARY. Together they collect SEVENTY PESOS — less than the hundred Lencho asked, but the most they can manage. He puts the money in an envelope addressed to Lencho and signs it simply 'GOD'. His response shows: (i) RESPECT for another's faith; (ii) PRACTICAL COMPASSION; (iii) HUMAN GENEROSITY across the divide of belief.

questions.question: Why is the ending of 'A Letter to God' considered ironic?
questions.answer: The ending is the central piece of irony. The very people who, MOVED BY LENCHO'S FAITH, contributed their own money to help him are accused by Lencho of being CROOKS who STOLE the missing thirty pesos. He calls them 'a bunch of crooks'. The reader sees what Lencho cannot — that the 'God' who answered his prayer is in fact a group of compassionate human beings, and that the 'thieves' are these very same people. So Lencho is BLIND TWICE: he doesn't see the human kindness behind the answer, and he projects greed onto the helpers. Irony is the gap between what the character thinks and what the reader knows; here the gap is total.

questions.question: Compare the characters of Lencho and the postmaster.
questions.answer: LENCHO is a hard-working farmer of unshakeable FAITH — he writes directly to God for 100 pesos and is sure his prayer will be answered. He is also STUBBORN and SUSPICIOUS — when only 70 pesos arrives he immediately accuses the post office staff. THE POSTMASTER is a fat, AMIABLE fellow whose first instinct is to LAUGH — but quickly he becomes serious, RESPECTING Lencho's faith. He is COMPASSIONATE, taking PRACTICAL action: he organises a collection from his employees and adds his own money. Both men are GOOD-HEARTED, but in different ways: Lencho's goodness is INTERNAL (faith) and the postmaster's is EXTERNAL (action). Sadly, Lencho cannot see that the postmaster's action is real goodness — and accuses him of theft.

questions.question: Identify three vocabulary words from 'A Letter to God' and give their meanings.
questions.answer: (i) HAILSTORM — a storm in which small balls of ice fall from the sky. (ii) CRESTFALLEN — sad and disappointed (literally, with a fallen crest, like a bird with drooping head). (iii) RESOLUTE — determined and firm. (iv) DELUGE — a heavy rain or flood. (v) CONVICTION — a firm belief. (vi) AMIABLE — good-tempered and friendly. Any three.

questions.question: Summarise the moment described in 'Dust of Snow' in your own words.
questions.answer: While walking under a HEMLOCK TREE, the speaker is suddenly dusted with FINE SNOW. The snow falls on him because a CROW has landed on a branch above and shaken loose the snow. That tiny, accidental gift — cold flakes from a bird often associated with bad luck on a tree often associated with sadness — somehow LIFTS HIS MOOD. A part of a day he had thought 'wasted' (he had RUED it) is given back to him. The poem is a single moment of UNEXPECTED EMOTIONAL CHANGE.

questions.question: Why does Frost choose a CROW and a HEMLOCK TREE for the imagery of 'Dust of Snow'?
questions.answer: In Western literary tradition, the CROW is often a symbol of bad luck, sadness or even death. The HEMLOCK TREE is a poisonous evergreen — in classical antiquity, hemlock was the poison given to Socrates. Both are 'dark' images. Frost CHOOSES them deliberately and then uses them to DELIVER joy — performing a quiet REVERSAL. The poem's message is: even the gloomy parts of life and nature can deliver UNEXPECTED blessings. By starting with these dark symbols, Frost makes the moment of joy more startling and more meaningful.

questions.question: What is the structure and rhyme scheme of 'Dust of Snow'?
questions.answer: 'Dust of Snow' is an EIGHT-LINE poem in TWO STANZAS of four lines each. It is a single sentence broken into two stanzas — a 'simple gift' offered by an unlikely source. The RHYME SCHEME is ABAB CDCD — a tight, controlled pattern. The lines are SHORT and almost casual; this simplicity matches the simplicity of the moment described. The compactness is part of the poem's power: a small idea expressed in a small form.

questions.question: What question does 'Fire and Ice' ask, and how does the speaker answer?
questions.answer: The poem asks how the world will end. There are two camps: those who say it will end in FIRE, those who say it will end in ICE. The SPEAKER first sides with the FIRE camp — drawing on what he has FELT of DESIRE — the hot, consuming kind. But, he says, if the world had to end TWICE, he knows enough of HATE to say that ICE would do for destruction too. So he answers: BOTH could end the world. Fire (desire) and ice (hate) are equally destructive — one fast and hot, the other slow and cold.

questions.question: How does Frost link two NATURAL forces with two HUMAN emotions?
questions.answer: Frost performs a striking link: FIRE = DESIRE; ICE = HATE. FIRE is HOT, CONSUMING and ALL-OR-NOTHING — like burning desire, lust, greed and unchecked ambition. ICE is SLOW, COLD and DEADENING — like the slow freezing of hate, indifference and bitterness. Both are NATURAL forces capable of physical destruction; Frost says both, as HUMAN emotions, are equally capable of DESTROYING WORLDS. The forces that end us are not asteroids or volcanoes — they are our own emotions. This is the essential insight: the apocalypse is INSIDE us.

questions.question: What is the structure and tone of 'Fire and Ice'?
questions.answer: 'Fire and Ice' is a NINE-LINE poem with a casual, conversational tone — phrases like 'Some say', 'From what I've tasted of desire', 'I think I know enough of hate' make it feel like the speaker is speaking aloud, not declaiming. The poem rhymes irregularly (roughly ABAABCBCB) but never lets rhyme dominate the meaning. The CONTRAST between fire and ice is the structural backbone. The CALM TONE contrasts powerfully with the apocalyptic content — making the poem more chilling, not less.

questions.question: Discuss 'A Letter to God' as a study of FAITH and IRONY. What does the story teach about human nature?
questions.answer: The story is built on TWO interlocking themes: FAITH and IRONY. LENCHO's FAITH is the story's engine. After the hailstorm destroys his crop, he turns not to neighbours, not to government, not to charity, but to GOD — directly, in a letter. His faith is so simple and so absolute that he names a specific amount and posts the letter to a non-existent address. This faith MOVES THE POSTMASTER and his employees, who do not share Lencho's religious world-view but who respect it. Their KINDNESS is not religious; it is HUMAN — practical, generous, anonymous. They collect 70 pesos out of their own pockets and send it as a reply 'from God'. So far the story is about the meeting of FAITH (Lencho) and COMPASSION (the postal staff). Then comes the IRONY. Lencho receives the money, sees it is 30 pesos short, and accuses the post office staff of stealing from God's gift. The very people who helped him are insulted by him. The reader sees what Lencho cannot — that his world-view, however genuine, is so RIGID that he cannot imagine an alternative explanation. WHAT THE STORY TEACHES — (i) Faith can be a source of strength but also of BLINDNESS — preventing us from seeing the kindness of those around us. (ii) Compassion in everyday people is real and powerful even when it goes UNRECOGNISED. (iii) Human beings are CAPABLE BOTH of generosity (the postmaster) and SUSPICION (Lencho) — sometimes in the same situation. (iv) IRONY is a way of telling truths that wouldn't be heard if stated directly: by showing Lencho's blindness, the story holds a mirror to our own. The story is small in length but large in implication.

questions.question: Discuss the message and craft of 'Dust of Snow'. Why is such a tiny moment worth a poem?
questions.answer: 'Dust of Snow' is a tiny poem about a tiny moment. Eight short lines, two stanzas, a single sentence — a snowflake-fall, a brief mood-change, and the poem ends. WHY DOES THIS MOMENT MATTER? Because it captures a TRUTH ABOUT HUMAN EXPERIENCE that big events often hide. Most days are NOT shaped by great triumphs or tragedies; they are shaped by SMALL SHIFTS — a kind word, a piece of music, a sudden breeze, a snowflake. Frost's poem says: a part of a day you had RUED can be SAVED by a tiny, accidental, unsought-for moment. CRAFT — Frost makes three choices that give the poem its quiet power. (i) He CHOOSES DARK SYMBOLS — the CROW (associated with bad luck) and the HEMLOCK TREE (associated with poison) — and then uses them to deliver JOY. This REVERSAL surprises the reader and signals the poem's deeper point: even the gloomy parts of life can carry blessings. (ii) He uses A SINGLE SENTENCE in two stanzas, with a tight ABAB CDCD rhyme scheme. This compactness mirrors the SHORTNESS of the moment described — the form enacts the content. (iii) He REFUSES TO MORALISE. He doesn't say 'always look for joy' or 'nature is healing'. He just records the moment. The reader has to do the work of finding the meaning — and that makes the meaning their own. WHY THIS IS WORTH A POEM — because most of life happens in moments like this, and a poet who can show us how to LOOK at them is teaching us how to LIVE in them.

questions.question: What is Frost's argument in 'Fire and Ice'? Why is it relevant today?
questions.answer: Frost's argument in 'Fire and Ice' is that the FORCES capable of ending a world are not natural disasters — they are HUMAN emotions. He links FIRE (HOT, CONSUMING) with DESIRE (greed, lust, ambition without limit) and ICE (COLD, SLOW, DEADENING) with HATE (bitterness, indifference, vengeance, the hardening of the heart). Both, he says, can DESTROY a world. The poem's calm, philosophical tone makes the argument all the more powerful — Frost is not panicking; he is OBSERVING. WHY RELEVANT TODAY? (i) CLIMATE CHANGE — driven by HUMAN DESIRE (consumption, growth at any cost) is FIRE in the literal and figurative sense. The world is heating up because of our refusal to limit our wants. (ii) WAR AND DIVISION — driven by HUMAN HATE (ethnic, religious, national hatreds, slow-burning grudges) is ICE — the cold freezing of compassion that allows us to see the 'other' as not-quite-human. From the World Wars to current conflicts, much of human destruction is the product of slow-frozen hate. (iii) PERSONAL LIFE — even at the smallest scale, our families, friendships and selves can be destroyed by uncontrolled DESIRE (for status, for things, for revenge) or by accumulated HATE (resentments, indifferences). Frost's poem is a warning at every scale — global, civic, personal. (iv) THE CHOICE IS OURS. The poem does not say one is worse than the other or that the apocalypse is inevitable. It just lays out the two paths and invites the reader to ASK WHICH ONE WE ARE WALKING. The poem is therefore not pessimistic — it is a CALL TO MORAL AWARENESS, asking us to control our own fire and our own ice before they end our world.

questions.question: What unifies 'A Letter to God', 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice' as a chapter? Discuss with examples.
questions.answer: At first glance the three pieces are very different — a Mexican short story about a farmer, a tiny New-England poem about a snowflake, and a philosophical poem about the end of the world. But the textbook places them together because they share a deep theme: SMALL THINGS HAVE GREAT POWER IN HUMAN LIFE. (i) IN 'A LETTER TO GOD', a single hour of HAILSTORM destroys a year's livelihood; a single LETTER addressed to God moves strangers to act with compassion; a single MISTAKE of judgement (Lencho accusing his benefactors) reveals how a person's whole character can collapse into bitterness. The story says: small EVENTS — a storm, a letter, a misjudgement — change everything. (ii) IN 'DUST OF SNOW', a tiny SNOWFALL from a crow's wing — the smallest physical event imaginable — is enough to REPAIR a person's mood for a day. Frost says: small MOMENTS of nature can heal us. (iii) IN 'FIRE AND ICE', tiny INTERNAL emotions — a flicker of desire, a freeze of hate — are scaled up to forces that can END A WORLD. Frost says: small EMOTIONS, fed and unchecked, become apocalyptic. CONNECTION — small EVENTS (story), small NATURAL MOMENTS (Dust of Snow), small INNER EMOTIONS (Fire and Ice). All three pieces show that the LARGE meaning of life — faith, mood, destruction, salvation — turns on SMALL hinges. The chapter teaches the careful reader to PAY ATTENTION to what is small, because that is where life actually happens. Across all three pieces, HUMAN BEINGS — with our faith, our compassion, our perception, our destructive emotions — are the centre of the action.

questions.question: Was the postmaster justified in deceiving Lencho? Defend your answer.
questions.answer: The postmaster's act of signing the envelope 'God' is both DECEPTIVE and KIND — and the question whether it was justified is genuinely complex. CASE FOR YES — (i) The postmaster's MOTIVE was pure: he wanted to PROTECT Lencho's faith and at the same time HELP him in his hour of need. (ii) The DECEPTION was a small one — he did not steal, lie about money, or deceive for his own benefit. (iii) He gave from his OWN salary; the cost of the deception fell on him, not on Lencho. (iv) Without the deception, Lencho would have known no one had answered — perhaps shaking his faith, leaving him without help. (v) Many ethical traditions (Christian, Jewish, Islamic, Buddhist) speak of WHITE LIES that protect the spirit of another while doing no harm. CASE FOR NO — (i) Lencho was DENIED the truth — the human compassion of the postmaster was not made known to him. (ii) Without knowing, Lencho ended up MISJUDGING the very people who helped him — calling them crooks. The deception led to the very BAD OUTCOME the postmaster had wanted to avoid (Lencho's bitterness). (iii) Long term, deceptions even with good intentions create distance between people. MY VIEW — the postmaster's intention was right, his action was kind, but his deception had unintended consequences. A more honest approach — telling Lencho that the post-office staff had collected the money out of admiration for his faith — might have produced gratitude AND preserved Lencho's faith in God's providence (working through human hands). The story therefore raises a sharp ethical question: even GOOD-HEARTED deception can backfire. The postmaster did the best he could think of in the moment, but the story leaves us to wonder if the truth would have served Lencho better.
